ch00.note: Xuantong (宣統) was the reign title of Puyi, the last emperor of the Qing dynasty, who came to the throne as a small child in 1908. Its second year corresponds to 1910 and its third to 1911; the dynasty fell in the revolution of 1911–1912, so these are the closing years of imperial China. The novel pairs each reign–year with its Western date, as here.

The pear blossom (梨花) is white, and in Chinese tradition its whiteness reads as purity, transience, and grief—white, not black, being the color of mourning. Because 梨 (‘pear’) sounds exactly like 离 (‘to part, to separate’), pear imagery has long shadowed stories of loss; the old taboo against splitting a pear to share it (分梨, homophone of 分离, ‘to part’) rests on the same pun. The blossom recurs through the novel as the token of the Yang family, and the prologue’s closing line, in which the Yangs’ pear blossom ‘bloomed strangely, bewitchingly bright’ over a night of burial and abduction, turns that beauty ominous. Corroborated.

The peony (牡丹) is the Chinese emblem of wealth and high rank, traditionally called the ‘flower of riches and honor’ (富贵花) and reckoned the king of flowers; worked in embroidery on a woman’s skirt it marks the wearer as a lady of a prosperous house, and its full spring bloom carries a further note of ripe feminine beauty. Corroborated; a standard motif of Chinese decorative art.

ch00.anchor: golden lotus embroidered on its side
ch00.note: A bound foot was called a ‘golden lotus’ (金莲), and the tiny embroidered silk slipper worn over it—like this pink, lotus-embroidered shoe—was its emblem. Foot-binding, practiced among Han Chinese women for roughly a thousand years, bent and crushed the foot from childhood to a length of a few inches; it was a mark of gentility and all but a precondition of a good marriage, and was only beginning to die out in the years this novel opens. Corroborated. The motif returns in the next chapter, where the Rong bride is named Jinlian, ‘golden lotus,’ yet has natural, unbound feet.

ch01.note: Bannermen (旗人) were members of the Eight Banners, the hereditary military and social organization of the Manchu Qing dynasty. To call the Rong family Bannermen marks them as part of the ruling Manchu caste—a caste that, in this year of 1911, stood on the very eve of the dynasty’s fall.

Red is the Chinese color of joy and good fortune, and above all the color of a wedding: for a marriage the house is hung with red silk and red lanterns, the bride arrives veiled in red in a red sedan chair, and the double-happiness character ‘囍’ is pasted on the doors. A great household on a wedding day would be red from gate to rooftop, exactly as here. (White, not black, is the Chinese color of mourning.) Corroborated; standard accounts of Chinese wedding custom.

The bride traveled to her wedding in a 花轿 (huajiao), a closed sedan chair draped in red and carried shoulder-high in procession with music and firecrackers; riding it was the emblem of a proper first marriage. Note the pointed contrast later in this chapter, when Second Madam is removed from the house in a hired ‘small sedan of blue satin’—the quiet, unfestive opposite of a bridal chair.

A wealthy Chinese household of this era could be polygynous. Beside the principal wife a man might take further consorts, ranked by order of entry — here First, Second, Third, and Fourth Madam (大太太, 二太太, and so on). At law the later consorts were concubines (妾) rather than wives, though a family like the Rongs styles them all ‘Madam’; their children all counted as the master’s, and rank governed precedence in the house. ‘Old Madam’ (老太太) is the master’s widowed mother, the matriarch, who outranks them all. The Republic’s civil code of 1929–1931 refused concubinage legal recognition, but the practice persisted well into the 1930s. Corroborated.

Jinlian (金莲) means ‘golden lotus,’ the conventional term for a woman’s bound foot. The name is pointed: this bride has natural, unbound feet (天足), and Master Rong prides himself on opposing foot-binding—so she is a ‘golden lotus’ that was never bound. The lotus embroidered on the muddied shoe in the Prologue belongs to the same motif.

Confucian rite required a son to mourn a parent for a nominal three years (in practice twenty-seven months): plain food and lodging, no festivities, no marriage, and marital abstinence. Officials left their posts for it (丁忧). The custom still carried real social force in the early Republic, which is why the family treats its breach as a catastrophe. Corroborated.

冷宫 (‘the cold palace’) is where an emperor’s disfavored consorts were shut away, out of sight and out of favor; by extension, any wife frozen out of her husband’s attention is said to live in the cold palace.

The narrator overstates the law here. The Qing Code (大清律例) did punish marrying or feasting during parental mourning, and a child conceived in mourning was a grave scandal; but the penalties were beatings and degradation, not death, and not confiscation of a family’s whole estate. What is true to life is the fear the passage actually turns on: a clan hungry for a rich house’s property could ruin it with an accusation. The legal claim as stated: contradicted; the social danger: corroborated.

Every birth year belongs to one of the twelve zodiac animals, and certain pairs are held to 犯冲—to clash, bringing ill luck if the two people live under one roof. Because the belief was widely honored, a declared clash was a socially unanswerable pretext for removing someone from a household, exactly how First Madam uses it here.

Folk belief held that the ghost of one who died by suicide or drowning could not pass on to rebirth until it found a 替身 (‘stand-in’): a living person induced to die the same death in its place. Hanging ghosts were especially feared for it. The country folk are saying Second Madam’s suicide was engineered by such a ghost—which is why the alternative rumor, that a living hand arranged it, sits so darkly beside the first.

灯花 (‘lamp-flower’) is the glowing bud of snuff that forms on a burning wick, read for centuries as an omen of coming good fortune. A wick budding double on the wedding night is doubly auspicious—an omen of children—and the line is also the novel’s discreet curtain over the consummation: the next sentence begins ‘A year later, a new life was born.’

ch01.anchor: a gold lock hung about his neck
ch01.note: A 长命锁 (‘longevity lock’), a lock-shaped pendant of gold or silver hung around a small child’s neck to ‘lock’ the child to life and bar early death. Buying one for her son is precisely the errand that has brought Fourth Madam out to the jewelry house—a protective charm, bought on the day the boy is taken.

ch01.anchor: withered like a yellow leaf in the west wind
ch01.note: The chapter title, 草木摇落露为霜 (‘grass and trees shed their leaves, and dew turns to frost’), is a line from the Yan ge xing (燕歌行, ‘Song of Yan’) by Cao Pi (187–226), long taken as the earliest complete seven-syllable-line poem in Chinese: the autumn wind is bleak, the weather cold; grass and trees shed their leaves, and dew turns to frost. Its images of autumn decline set the key for a chapter of deaths, a lost child, and a withered wife.
月亮门, a circular opening in a Chinese garden wall, framing the view beyond like a full moon; a standard feature of a great house’s courtyards.

ch01.anchor: the adopted son of Fourth Madam
ch01.note: Strictly a 干儿子, a ‘nominal son’ or godson: a recognized, affectionate kinship tie sealed by gifts and forms of address, but not legal adoption into the line of descent. The distinction matters: the foundling can bear the lost boy’s name and live as Fourth Madam’s son while standing, in law and in inheritance, outside the Rong line.

ch02.note: Historically accurate. The Manifesto of the Communist Party was first published in London in February 1848; the 1888 English edition mentioned just below—translated by Samuel Moore and edited by Engels—is likewise real. The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen to which Cong Feng compares it was adopted in 1789, during the French Revolution.

Lin Daiyu—and the other names in this passage: Jia Tanchun, Xue Baochai, Shi Xiangyun, Qingwen, Siqi, Xiren, Yuanyang—are all figures in the eighteenth-century novel Dream of the Red Chamber (红楼梦). Lishui flatters herself with the young ladies’ sensitivity, talent, shrewdness and grace; A-Chu privately assigns her the maidservants’ sharp tongues and pride instead. The whole comparison is lost on a reader who does not know the book.

The chapter title, 朝生春晖暮留霭 (‘born at dawn to spring’s light, wrapped in mist by dusk’), turns on 春晖, ‘spring sunlight’—a classical figure for a mother’s love, from Meng Jiao’s (751–814) Youzi yin (游子吟, ‘Song of the Wandering Son’), which asks how the heart of an inch-long blade of grass can ever repay the light of three spring months. It is Fourth Madam’s maternal hold, not the abstract authority of the Rong house, that binds the wandering A-Chu.

ch02.anchor: household servant of a special sort
ch02.note: A 家奴 (jianu), literally a ‘house slave,’ was a hereditary bond-servant belonging to a household—not a hired domestic free to leave, but a person owned by the family, whether through debt, sale, or being taken in as a foundling. That A-Chu is a jianu, however well educated and however loosely called a ‘foster son,’ is the fact that governs his whole predicament: he is chattel of the Rong house, bound by ownership as much as by gratitude. Corroborated; such bond-servitude persisted in wealthy Chinese households into the Republican era.

The source has A-Chu schooled first at a 私塾 (sishu), the traditional private school where boys learned the Confucian classics by memorization and recitation, and then at a 洋学堂 (yang xuetang), a ‘foreign-style school’ teaching a modern Western curriculum. The move from the one to the other traces the great educational divide of the early twentieth century, as classical learning gave way to Western science—here, the Western medicine A-Chu goes on to take up. Corroborated.

The xiao (箫) is a vertical, end-blown bamboo flute with a soft, breathy, melancholy tone, quite distinct from the transverse dizi; it is traditionally the instrument of solitude and grief. Rong Sheng’s playing of it recurs through the novel as the emblem of his ruined and mournful life. Corroborated.

Opium—smoked through a long pipe over a small lamp—was epidemic in China from the nineteenth century onward, and a wealthy idler like Rong Sheng sinking into addiction abroad is wholly of its time; the drug ruined countless fortunes, and its suppression ran through the whole Republican period. As a Western-trained doctor, A-Chu manages the craving with measured injections of morphine, then itself used to wean opium addicts. Corroborated.

ch02.anchor: Confucian doctrine of gratitude and repayment
ch02.note: Confucian ethics laid heavy stress on 报恩 (bao’en), the duty to repay a debt of kindness—above all the debt a child owes for having been raised, which shades into filial piety itself. It is this obligation, more than any law, that chains A-Chu to the Rong household and to Fourth Madam, who took him in off the street; Cong Feng is charging him with letting that inherited duty devour his freedom and his youth. Corroborated.

ch03.anchor: sunk in the pond to drown
ch03.note: Chen tang (沉塘), ‘sinking in the pond,’ was a lineage punishment in old rural China: an offender against sexual morality—an adulterer, or a couple who eloped—might be bound and drowned in a village pond on the clan’s authority. Rong Sheng invokes it to measure how far England lies from home.

The source here reads 威尔逊卡迪芙 (‘Wilson Cardiff’). Cardiff is the capital of Wales (威尔士), and 威尔逊 (Wilson) appears to be a slip in the source for 威尔士; it is rendered simply as Cardiff throughout, as elsewhere in the book.

The chapter title, 同林春鸟各自飞 (‘birds of the same wood each take flight’), invokes the folk saying husband and wife are birds of the same wood; when calamity comes, each flies its own way (夫妻本是同林鸟，大难临头各自飞). The chapter scatters its pairs: A-Chu turns back from Cong Hui to save a stranger’s child, and Cong Hui reaches the harbour only to find him already gone.

ch03.anchor: an enemy from five hundred years ago
ch03.note: The phrase renders 五百年前的冤家. A 冤家 (yuanjia) is a fated adversary—an enemy one is karmically bound to—and the word carries a wry undertone, since it doubles as an affectionate term for a lover or a maddening intimate. ‘Five hundred years’ invokes the folk notion that the ties of this life, love and enmity alike, were fixed by a connection in a former one. Corroborated.

To make someone kneel (下跪) was to force from the body its own admission of inferiority: kneeling belonged to the lesser before the greater—servant before master, child before parent, subject before throne—and to command it, as Lishui does here and Rong Sheng does moments later, is to press the full weight of that hierarchy onto A-Chu. That a Western-trained doctor still kneels on command measures how completely the bond-servant’s station has survived his education. Corroborated.

ch03.anchor: a weakened body cannot take tonics
ch03.note: In Chinese medicine 补药 (buyao), ‘tonics’ or restoratives, are taken to replenish the body’s vital forces; but a classic maxim holds 虚不受补—a body too depleted cannot ‘receive’ a tonic, so that dosing a ruined constitution only harms it further. Rong Sheng has turned exactly this against himself, pouring tonic after tonic into an already broken body so that his self-willed decline would pass for natural sickness. Corroborated; standard traditional-medicine doctrine.

ch04.note: Juntong (军统) is shorthand for the Bureau of Investigation and Statistics of the Nationalist Military Affairs Commission, the Kuomintang’s secret-police and intelligence service. Strictly, it bore that name only from 1938; in 1931 its institutional forebears were just taking shape, so the term is used a little anachronistically here. The Communist Special Branch (特科) on the other side, however, was real and active in Shanghai from 1927, which fits the novel’s date exactly.

The two codenames are drawn from classical nature-images. Piaofeng (飘风, ‘whirlwind, drifting wind’) echoes the Daodejing: a whirlwind does not last a whole morning. Shiyu (时雨, ‘timely rain’) is the seasonable rain of the classics, falling just when it is needed. Wind and rain, the storm about to break, run all through this chapter’s talk of ‘a storm tonight.’

The chapter title, 阴差阳错难提防 (‘by a cross-grained twist of fate, hard to guard against’), rests on the idiom 阴差阳错—literally a ‘yin-error, yang-mistake,’ a chain of small chances that throws everything awry. The chapter runs on such accidents: a lost admission notice, a stranger’s helping hand, and a crate that proves to be nothing like what it seems.

An ‘iron rooster’ (铁公鸡) is a skinflint—the full saying runs ‘an iron rooster, from which not a single feather can be plucked.’ Muci is teasing Lao Yu that coaxing this notorious tightwad into spending money (into ‘bleeding a little’) is a rare event indeed. Corroborated; a common idiom.

After the Nationalists and Communists broke apart in 1927 in a bloody purge—the ‘White Terror,’ whose slaughter of Communists in Shanghai that April all but destroyed the Party in the cities—the CCP survived there only as a deep clandestine network. To be an exposed underground Communist in the Shanghai of 1931 meant near-certain arrest and death, which is why Muci must sever every tie, his family included, and disappear behind a forged story. Corroborated.

The ‘Soviet areas’ (苏区) were the rural base territories the Communists governed in the countryside—above all the Central Soviet in Jiangxi—where the Red Army held ground and the Party ran a miniature state of its own. To ‘go to the front’ and reach the Soviet areas is what Muci longs for: open revolutionary struggle, rather than the lonely deep-cover work he is instead being ordered into. Corroborated.

ch05.note: The chapter title, 时人不识凌云木 (‘the people of the day know not the cloud-piercing tree’), and the couplet Du Luning recites are from the quatrain Xiao song (小松, ‘The Little Pine’) by the late-Tang poet Du Xunhe (杜荀鹤, 846–904): from small a prickly seedling deep in the grass, and now little by little it clears the weeds; the people of the day know not the cloud-piercing tree, till it has pierced the cloud, and then they call it high. Long read as the poet’s self-portrait, it turns on the failure to recognize greatness before it is obvious—exactly Du Luning’s point about the untried Yang Muci. Where the received text reads 直待 (‘wait until’), the novel quotes 直到 (‘until’).

ch05.anchor: Is it not a joy to learn
ch05.note: Du Luning opens with the first lines of the Analects of Confucius (论语 1.1): Is it not a joy to learn and to practice in season what one has learned? Is it not a delight to have friends come from afar? Is he not a gentleman who feels no rancor though others take no note of him? The ‘Sayings of Master Zeng’ he quotes a moment later—each day I examine myself on three points—are Analects 1.4, the words of Confucius’s disciple Zengzi (曾子). That a spymaster should recast the Confucian program of self-cultivation as a lesson in obscurity and infiltration is the passage’s deliberate irony.

‘Director Dai’ is Dai Li (戴笠, 1897–1946), head of the Nationalists’ military-intelligence apparatus and one of the most feared men in Republican China, sometimes called ‘China’s Himmler.’ His formal command of the Juntong dates only from its founding in 1938; naming him here, in a scene set in 1931, is of a piece with the novel’s slightly early use of ‘Juntong’ (see the note at Chapter 4).

The phrase renders 山雨欲来风满楼, a line by the late-Tang poet Xu Hun (许浑) from his poem on the east tower of Xianyang: as a mountain storm gathers, the wind rises and fills the high tower. It has become the proverbial image for the oppressive tension that goes before an upheaval—here at once the literal weather and the political storm breaking over the whole chapter. Corroborated.

ch06.note: Gege (格格) was a Manchu title borne by daughters of the Qing imperial house and higher nobility, roughly ‘princess’ or ‘young lady of rank.’ To nickname He Yashan ‘He Gege’ is to mark her, half in earnest and half in mockery, as a scion of the fallen Qing aristocracy—the ‘old Qing loyalists and their heirs’ (清朝遗老遗少) of the sentence before.

‘Save the children’ (救救孩子) is the famous closing cry of Lu Xun’s A Madman’s Diary (狂人日记, 1918), the founding story of modern Chinese fiction, where it is the diarist’s last hope that a generation not yet made cannibal might still be spared. In He Yashan’s mouth the words carry that literary charge—a plea against a devouring world—beneath their plain surface.

The chapter title, 宫花旋落已成尘 (‘the palace blossom, swiftly fallen, is already dust’), draws on the ‘palace flower’ (宫花) of Tang verse—the blossom in the deserted palace that stands for youth and beauty spent unseen, as in Yuan Zhen’s Xing gong (行宫): lonely, the old traveling-palace; its palace flowers red in silence. The exact line does not appear to be a quotation from any single canonical poem; it works rather as an echo of that whole tradition, bodied out here in the two young lovers cut down and in the fainting girl Rong Sheng sees fall like a flower.

‘The judge of horses had met his thousand-li steed’ renders 伯乐总算遇到了千里马: Bole (伯乐) was the legendary judge of horses of antiquity, and a ‘thousand-li horse’ (千里马) one that could run a thousand li in a day—together a byword for a discerning patron who recognizes rare talent, Du Luning casting himself as Bole to Yang Muci’s steed. In the digital source a stray line of pirate-website advertising (‘阳光中文网 www.sunshe.com…’) is appended to this sentence; it belongs to the file, not the novel, and is kept verbatim in the bilingual record but left out of the reading text.

Shanghai’s elite girls’ schools—St. Mary’s Hall (圣玛利亚女校) above all, the famous Episcopalian school where the writer Eileen Chang would later study—educated the daughters of the wealthy and Westernized in English, music, and Western manners, and were a badge of the highest social polish. (The ‘Hongxia’ school named beside it is the novel’s invention.) A girl bred at such a school could be expected to waltz, which is exactly what Muci is fishing for. Corroborated for St. Mary’s.

The paper butterflies are an unmistakable sign. In the beloved folk legend of the Butterfly Lovers (梁山伯与祝英台), two lovers parted in life are buried together and their souls rise from the grave as a joined pair of butterflies—China’s very archetype of 殉情, dying for love. By cutting out two butterflies and laying them on the dead couple, the silent Yu Xiaojiang names Guo Ziqiong and He Yashan lovers united at last in death. Corroborated.

A-Chu makes a 长揖 (changyi): the traditional Chinese salute of respect, made standing, hands clasped together and swept from high before the face down to the waist in a deep bow. Deliberately old-fashioned and courteous, it sets his gracious formality against the scrum of flashbulbs and shouted questions. Corroborated.

The 土地庙 is the shrine of the 土地公, the local earth-god—the humblest and most ubiquitous deity of Chinese folk religion, a minor tutelary spirit with a small shrine in almost every village and neighborhood. A-Fu’s grumble that the reporters have ‘sprung from who knows what little earth-god’s temple’ casts them as small fry crawling out of every cranny, the way such shrines dot the land. Corroborated.

The Bund (外滩) is the grand waterfront along the Huangpu River, lined with the banks and trading houses of the foreign concessions; by extension 上海滩, ‘the Shanghai shore,’ came to stand for the whole glittering, cut-throat world of the city—its finance, its glamour, and its gangland alike. Lishui’s imagined headline casts Rong Sheng as a gallant of that world in the stock role of the ‘hero who rescues the beauty’ (英雄救美). Corroborated.

ch07.note: The chapter title, 却疑春色在邻家 (‘and I half-suspect the spring’s colors are next door’), is the closing line of Yu qing (雨晴, ‘Clearing After Rain’) by the late-Tang poet Wang Jia (王驾): before the rain, first the buds seen among the flowers; after the rain, not a flower left beneath the leaves; the bees and butterflies in a throng go over the wall—and I half-suspect the spring’s colors are next door. Its wistfulness—beauty always just elsewhere, just out of reach—keys a chapter of longings deflected and a homecoming that rings a little hollow. (The widely printed ‘蜂蝶纷纷…却疑’ wording is the version polished by Wang Anshi.)

‘The Old Buddha’ (老佛爷) was the customary honorific for the Empress Dowager Cixi (慈禧, 1835–1908), who dominated the late-Qing court for nearly half a century. Fourth Madam’s unfinished boast—that she once attended the Old Buddha—places her, before her life in the Rong house, among the palace women of the last imperial reigns.

ch07.anchor: the pearls had returned to Hepu
ch07.note: ‘The pearls had returned to Hepu’ renders the idiom 合浦珠还. Hepu (合浦), a southern coastal commandery famous in Han times for its pearl fisheries, was said to have lost its oysters when grasping officials over-harvested them, and to have seen them return only when an upright governor, Meng Chang, restored good rule (Book of the Later Han). Ever since, the phrase has meant the recovery of something precious once lost—here, First Madam’s son restored to her.

ch07.anchor: the advertisement girls on a New Year print
ch07.note: A New Year print (年画, nianhua) is a brightly colored woodblock picture pasted up at the lunar New Year for luck—plump children, door-gods, goddesses of plenty. By the 1930s Shanghai’s printers had wedded the old form to advertising, turning out posters of rosy, near-identical ‘New Year girls’ to sell cigarettes and soap. To liken the maids to such girls is to call them uniformly, mass-producedly pretty. Corroborated.

To kowtow (磕头, ketou, ‘knock the head’) is to kneel and touch the forehead to the ground, the deepest of ritual obeisances—owed by child to parent, servant to master, the living to the ancestors. First Madam waives it (‘no need to hold to the old rules’) because a foreign-trained doctor now stands above such servility; Fourth Madam insists on it all the same, as the repayment of a debt of kindness that binds the bond-servant. Corroborated.

Reporting the family’s doings to its ancestors—here a son’s safe return—is a central act of Chinese domestic religion. Before the ancestral tablets the family burns incense, bows, and announces births, marriages, homecomings, and deaths, so that the dead share in the fortunes of the living and go on watching over the line. It is Confucian filial piety made visible: the dead are not gone but present, and owed the same duty as the living elders. Corroborated.

Qingming (清明, ‘Clear and Bright’), the tomb-sweeping festival of early April, is the day families visit the ancestral graves to weep, clear the weeds, lay out food and wine, and burn paper money for the dead. It is the great spring rite of remembrance; Rong Sheng’s promise to come ‘after Qingming’ sets the season for the graveside scenes to follow. Corroborated.

The Tongji Hospital (同济医院) grew from the German-founded medical school set up in Shanghai in 1907 by the physician Erich Paulun; by the 1920s it was among China’s foremost institutions of Western medicine. That A-Chu, trained abroad, practices there places him at the leading edge of the modern, foreign-derived medicine that was displacing the classical Chinese pharmacy of his own adoptive family. Corroborated.

Guanyin (观音), the Bodhisattva of Compassion, is the most beloved deity of Chinese Buddhism—the merciful being who hears the cries of the world, popularly worshipped in female form as the goddess of mercy. To ‘build bridges and mend roads’ (修桥铺路) is the stock phrase for pious charitable works that earn merit. Rong Sheng is calling A-Chu, half-fondly and half-mockingly, a soft-hearted living saint who can refuse no one in need. Corroborated.

ch08.note: The chapter title, 前度杨郎今又来 (‘Young Yang of former days comes again’), reworks the closing line of Liu Yuxi’s (刘禹锡, 772–842) quatrain Revisiting the Xuandu Temple (再游玄都观): the hundred-mu courtyard half moss now, the peach blossom all gone and the rape-flower come; where is he now, the Daoist who planted the peaches? Liu of former days comes again (前度刘郎今又来). Liu wrote it in 828, on returning to the capital after fourteen years’ banishment that an earlier poem on the same temple had provoked—a flourish of unbroken defiance. Swapping 杨 (Yang) for 刘 (Liu) bends that homecoming to A-Chu’s own: the young man of Yang blood coming back, all unknowing, to the Yang house. The attribution is corroborated.

‘A leopard-cat exchanged for the crown prince’ (狸猫换太子) is the celebrated story, popularized by the Qing novel The Three Heroes and Five Gallants (三侠五义) and the opera stage, in which a jealous palace consort has a newborn prince—the future Emperor Renzong of Song—secretly swapped at birth for a skinned wildcat, so that the true heir is cast out and reared in obscurity. Rongrong lets the phrase slip because it fits A-Chu too well: a child of unknown origin in a great house, and, as the reader half-guesses, not the foundling he is taken to be. The tale is legend, not history.

ch08.anchor: the darkest spot right beneath the lamp
ch08.note: ‘The dark beneath the lamp’ (灯下黑) is a common saying: an oil lamp throws its light outward and leaves its own base in shadow, so the spot nearest the flame is the least watched. In tradecraft it is the hiding place in plain sight—here, a hunted man sheltering in the basement of a newspaper office the authorities would never think to search.

The qipao (旗袍, also ‘cheongsam’) is the close-fitting, high-collared, side-slit dress that became the signature garment of the fashionable modern woman in the Shanghai of the 1920s and 1930s. Recut from the loose Manchu banner-gown to sheathe the figure, it marked its wearer as urban, stylish, and up to date. Corroborated.

Longjing (龙井, ‘Dragon Well’) is a celebrated green tea from the hills above Hangzhou, long the most prized of Chinese teas and a mark of refinement and means. To serve it freshly steeped is to set a table of quiet luxury. Corroborated.

The ‘white medicine’ (白药, baiyao) is a traditional Chinese styptic powder—most famously Yunnan Baiyao, compounded from herbs—sprinkled on a wound to stanch bleeding and speed healing. That the Western-trained A-Chu reaches for it alongside anesthetic and alcohol is a small emblem of the two medicines meeting in one pair of hands. Corroborated.

The Shanghai Garrison Command (淞沪警备司令部) was the Nationalist military authority policing the Chinese-administered parts of the city; through the early 1930s it was a chief instrument of the ‘white terror,’ hunting, arresting, and executing Communists. Its cars converging on the newspaper office are the state closing in on Lao Yu. Corroborated.

A small anachronism. In 1931 the Communists’ central base was the rural Soviet in Jiangxi (see the note on the Soviet areas, Chapter 4); Yan’an (延安), in Shaanxi, became the Party’s headquarters only after the Long March, from 1935–1937 onward. The novel names the later, more famous capital of the revolution in place of the base that would actually have received Shanghai’s wireless traffic at this date.

ch09.anchor: as though he himself were the dead infant
ch09.note: The chapter title, 开门人即闭门人 (‘the one who opens the door is the one who closed it’), echoes a Chan Buddhist verse attached by legend to the philosopher Wang Yangming (王阳明, 1472–1529): visiting a monastery, he is said to have found a sealed room bearing his own name on a dead monk’s spirit-tablet and the lines fifty years hence, Wang Yangming; open the door and it is still the man who closed it (开门犹是闭门人)—a parable of rebirth, the self returning to a threshold it once shut behind it. A-Chu opening the shrine doors upon the dead child’s altar carries the same charge of one identity crossing the boundary of death. The verse is folk legend rather than documented fact.

‘Gallant of the Crimson Bower’ (怡红公子) is the studio-sobriquet of Jia Baoyu, the pampered hero of Cao Xueqin’s Dream of the Red Chamber (红楼梦), after his garden apartment the Court of Crimson Joy (怡红院). For the dissolute Tang Shaoli to style himself so is pure self-flattery—claiming Baoyu’s charm while owning only his idleness. (The ‘five poisons,’ 五毒, are the stock vices of the wastrel: feasting, drink, whoring, gambling, and opium.)

The Aisin Gioro (爱新觉罗) were the ruling clan of the Qing dynasty. Aisin means ‘gold’ in Manchu, and after the dynasty fell in 1911 many of the clan took the Han surname Jin (金, ‘gold’)—the sense kept, the Manchu form dropped. A-Chu’s point is that even the emperors’ own kinsmen are commoners now, and Tang Shaoli’s talk of ‘upper sorts’ is an anachronism. Corroborated.

A spirit-tablet (灵牌 or 牌位) is an upright wooden tablet inscribed with a dead person’s name—here ‘Spirit-Seat of Yang Muchu’—believed to house the soul and to be the focus of offerings: the incense, fruit, and flowers set before it in this little shrine. Households kept such tablets for their ancestors on a domestic altar and tended them as the abiding presence of the dead. That a family should enshrine a photograph and tablet for a child said to have died in infancy is the first sign that his death is not what it seems. Corroborated.

The death-day (祭日, jiri) is the anniversary of a death, kept each year with mourning and offerings to the dead—a fixed occasion of the domestic ancestral cult, quite apart from any birthday. Madam Yang’s anguish is that her daughter’s birthday falls on the very day she must instead mourn her son. Corroborated.

ch10.anchor: cut the flower of one heart by mistake
ch10.note: The chapter title, 误剪同心一片花 (‘by error the flower of one heart is cut’), turns on 同心—the 同心结, or ‘heart-knit knot,’ a looped love-token that Tang poets made a byword for constant love (Chao Cai’s Midnight Songs: . . . and tie it into a heart-knit knot, 绾作同心结), and by extension the 同心花, the twin-lobed ‘flower of one heart.’ To ‘cut’ it by mistake is to sever a bond of joined hearts unawares—A-Chu’s figure for Rong Sheng, who, fleeing his own past, lets a warped affection snip the love that was his. The line is not a traceable single quotation but is built in the classical manner from this love-knot imagery (cf. Li He’s Su Xiaoxiao’s Grave: 无物结同心，烟花不堪剪).

ch10.anchor: hardest of all to nurse oneself through
ch10.note: A-Chu quotes Li Qingzhao (李清照, 1084–c. 1155), the greatest of the Song ci poets: the season when it is warm one moment and cold the next is hardest of all to nurse oneself through (乍暖还寒时候，最难将息), from her Sheng sheng man (声声慢). The lyric is a widow’s lament, and the doctor’s tag—ostensibly mere seasonal counsel—carries for the reader the poem’s undertow of loss, set against the wounded, self-deceiving He Yashu. Corroborated.

The Duke of Windsor was Edward VIII (1894–1972), who in December 1936, less than a year on the British throne, abdicated to marry the twice-divorced American Wallis Simpson—giving up, as A-Chu says, the realm for love. The broad triangular ‘Windsor knot’ is named for him; by most accounts, however, he never tied one, achieving his full-knotted look with specially thick-lined ties knotted four-in-hand. The abdication is corroborated; the knot’s attribution to him is the popular story rather than his own practice.

ch10.anchor: slipped off her own jade bracelet
ch10.note: Jade (玉) was the most treasured of stones in China, an emblem of purity, virtue, and constancy; a jade bangle, worn snug on the wrist and not easily drawn off, was a woman’s intimate, lifelong ornament, often a betrothal or love token. For He Yashu to leave hers in A-Chu’s pocket is thus a charged, deliberately compromising gift—which is why its reappearance can be turned into a threat to her name. Corroborated.

The French Park (法国公园, today’s Fuxing Park) lay in the French Concession—one of the foreign-governed districts, with the International Settlement, carved out of Shanghai by treaty in the nineteenth century. Within them foreign law ran and Chinese jurisdiction did not, and a European leisure of parks, cafes, and afternoon tea flourished. This extraterritorial city is at once the playground of the novel’s rich and the covering shadow in which its spies can work. Corroborated.

In Chinese medicine health is a balance of heat and cold, and remedies are classed to match: a ‘warming, restorative’ (温补) prescription of tonic herbs is meant to build up a depleted, ‘cold’ constitution. Such a prescription is not swallowed as a pill but simmered down at home into a bitter decoction—the ‘decocting’ A-Chu goes on to explain. That a Western-trained doctor writes one shows how far the two medical worlds overlapped in practice. Corroborated.

ch11.anchor: the fortunes of his life, adrift like duckweed
ch11.note: The chapter title, 平生际遇似萍飘 (‘a whole life’s fortunes drift like duckweed’), is the opening line of the fortune-oracle quatrain A-Chu draws at the Ciyun Temple, whose closing line in turn furnishes the title of Chapter 12. It is not a quotation from any single poem but is built in the classical manner on the old image of the duckweed (萍)—rootless, carried wherever the water takes it—for a life at the mercy of chance; compare Wen Tianxiang (文天祥, 1236–1283), Crossing Lingding Yang (过零丁洋): the land is torn like willow-down scattered on the wind, this life afloat and sinking like duckweed beaten by the rain (身世浮沉雨打萍). The whole oracle also foretells the plot: the foundling who has ‘mistaken the strange land for home.’

ch11.anchor: a one-horned beast of legend from high antiquity
ch11.note: A-Chu is unpacking the archaic graph 灋 for 法 (‘law’). The Shuowen jiezi (说文解字, c. 100 CE) defines it: 灋 is punishment; it is level as water, and so takes the water radical; the 廌 is what gores the crooked and drives it away. The 廌 (zhì) is the 獬豸 (xièzhì), a mythical one-horned beast that butts the guilty party in a dispute; from antiquity it was an emblem of justice, its image worn on the caps and robes of the censorate. A-Chu’s gloss is thus exact—and Ronghua’s retort, why then does he not butt, turns the etymology against his own submission. Corroborated.

ch11.anchor: Let there be, beside the gate of the grave, young life at play
ch11.note: Rong Sheng quotes the close of Pushkin’s lyric of 1829, Whether I Wander Along Noisy Streets (Брожу ли я вдоль улиц шумных): and let young life play at the entrance of the grave, and let indifferent nature shine on in beauty everlasting. The lines console by setting fresh life against death’s very door—a bleak comfort in the mouth of the jilted Rong Sheng. Corroborated.

ch11.anchor: One cannot know the true face of Mount Lu
ch11.note: A-Chu quotes the closing couplet of Su Shi’s (苏轼, 1037–1101) quatrain Written on the Wall of Xilin Temple (题西林壁): one cannot know the true face of Mount Lu, only because one stands within this very mountain. The poem’s point—that whoever is caught inside a thing cannot see its whole shape—is doubly apt for a man who cannot yet read his own origins. (The received text has 只缘, ‘only because’; the novel quotes 只因, of the same sense.) Corroborated.

‘Family discipline’ (家法, jiafa) was the recognized power of a household head to punish his own—wives, children, servants, bond-servants—on his own authority, a private penal jurisdiction the state left largely untouched; the word also names the very rod kept for the purpose. Rong Sheng’s ordering A-Chu to strike his own face is this power in action, and it stands in bitter counterpoint to the character for ‘law’ (法), whose just meaning A-Chu expounds later in the same chapter. Corroborated.

Drawing lots (求签) is a common temple divination: the worshipper shakes a cylinder of numbered bamboo slips until one falls out, then exchanges its number for a printed slip of verse—here read by the old nun—whose cryptic lines are taken to foretell his fortune. The quatrain A-Chu draws maps his whole predicament, and its last line furnishes the title of the next chapter. Corroborated.

Bird’s nest (燕窝)—the hardened saliva with which swiftlets build their nests, painstakingly cleaned and stewed—is among the costliest of Chinese delicacies, prized as a nourishing tonic; white (silver) fungus (银耳) is a similarly esteemed restorative. Simmered into a sweet soup, it is at once a luxury and a token of tender care, which is what Chan’er’s late-night bowl for A-Chu conveys. Corroborated.

A-Chu is contrasting the conventions of Chinese brush painting (国画) with Western art. In place of the single fixed vanishing point of European perspective, the Chinese scroll uses a ‘scattered’ or moving viewpoint (散点透视), letting the eye travel through a scene from many positions at once, and it builds form through line and ink rather than by Western shading and volume. The pictures are done in ink and mineral color on absorbent xuan paper with a soft animal-hair brush—the tools laid out on this desk. Corroborated.

ch11.anchor: Where things are not level, they cry out
ch11.note: Ronghua is playing on a famous line of the Tang essayist Han Yu (韩愈, 768–824): it is the general rule of things that they cry out when they cannot find their balance (大凡物不得其平则鸣). Han Yu meant it of writers driven to speak by injustice and hardship; Ronghua turns it, by way of the ink she has just splashed, into a goad—the wronged should protest, so why does A-Chu not? Corroborated.

ch12.anchor: what day shall he go home to wash the traveller’s robe
ch12.note: The chapter title, 何日归家洗客袍 (‘what day shall I go home to wash the traveller’s robe?’), is the closing line of the Chapter 11 oracle quatrain, and is lifted verbatim from the ci Yi jian mei: Passing Wujiang by Boat (一剪梅·舟过吴江) by the Song poet Jiang Jie (蒋捷, c. 1245–c. 1305): what day shall I go home to wash the traveller’s robe? Tune the silver-charactered pipes, burn the heart-shaped incense . . . Jiang Jie wrote as a man stranded far from home after the fall of the Song; the ‘traveller’s robe’ carries the wanderer’s ache to return, which here becomes the foundling A-Chu’s own. Corroborated.

ch12.anchor: Pear blossoms fall, apricot blossoms open
ch12.note: The tanci lyric Fourth Madam sings is the aria of Jiao Guiying (敫桂英) from The Ardent Probe (情探), the stage version of the old tale Wang Kui Betrays Guiying (王魁负桂英, out of the Fenxiang ji): abandoned by the scholar she once saved and raised to office, Guiying kills herself and returns as a ghost to reproach him. Her lament—pear blossoms fall, apricot blossoms open . . . I gaze till my eyes break through the autumn waters, and not one letter comes—is sung by that ghost, which is why A-Chu, a moment later, calls the song ‘ghost-talk’ and names Jiao Guiying and The Ardent Probe. The chill he feels is the song’s, and the plot’s.

The Third Communist International, or Comintern (共产国际), was the Moscow-based federation of Communist parties founded by Lenin in 1919; the Chinese Communist Party was affiliated with it from its founding in 1921. For Cong Feng to have ‘gone to the Soviet Union and joined the Third International’ marks him, in the eyes of the Nationalist police of the novel’s Shanghai, as a revolutionary of the most dangerous stripe. Corroborated.

Amitabha (阿弥陀佛, Emituofo) is the Buddha of Boundless Light who presides over the Western Paradise, the Pure Land; reciting his name is the central devotion of Pure Land Buddhism, the most popular form of the faith in China. Spoken aloud as here, it serves as a pious exclamation—a breath of blessing, resignation, or thanks, roughly ‘mercy be’—rather than a statement. The scarred old nun studs her fortune-telling with it to mark each utterance as devout. Corroborated.

ch12.anchor: putting an innocent man to the block
ch12.note: A-Chu translates the grim phrase 宰白鸭, ‘to slaughter a white duck.’ Under the late Qing it named a real abuse of justice: a poor man was paid to confess to a capital crime he had not committed and go to execution in the true culprit’s place, so that a wealthy killer went free and the magistrate closed his case. To shoot men merely to fill an arrest quota, A-Chu says, is that same murder of the innocent under another name. Corroborated.

Pingtan (评弹) is the storytelling-and-ballad art of Suzhou and the lower Yangzi, performed in the soft Wu dialect: one or two performers narrate and sing a long romantic tale to their own accompaniment on the pipa, a pear-shaped lute, and the three-stringed sanxian. The sung portion is tanci. Long prized by the Jiangnan gentry as the most refined of popular entertainments, it is heard in the teahouse ‘storytelling houses’ (书场) like the one later in this chapter. Corroborated.

ch12.anchor: the Herd-Boy and the Weaving-Maid stars
ch12.note: The Herd-Boy (牵牛, the star Altair) and the Weaving-Maid (织女, Vega) are the lovers of China’s best-loved star-legend: a mortal cowherd and a heavenly weaving-girl, married and then parted to opposite banks of the Milky Way, allowed to meet only once a year, on the seventh night of the seventh month, over a bridge of magpies. To watch their stars is to sigh over love kept apart—here the concubine Xu Yuzhen’s longing for a love she is denied. Corroborated.

A ‘top-graduate’ renders 状元 (zhuangyuan), the scholar who placed first in the palace examination at the summit of the imperial civil service—the highest honor the old system could bestow, and the storybook ideal of a husband, a poor student raised at a stroke to fame and office. The examinations were abolished in 1905, a few years before the events the singers tell, but 状元及第, ‘to pass as top graduate,’ lived on as a set phrase for the perfect match. The concubine sings that she wants no such glory, only love. Corroborated.

ch13.note: The chapter title, 琵琶声泣血泪仇 (‘the pipa’s cry weeps blood, a feud of tears’), is not a quotation but plays on the long tradition of the pipa as the instrument of lament, crowned by Bai Juyi’s (白居易, 772–846) Song of the Pipa (琵琶行, 816), in which a courtesan’s playing on a river barge moves the whole company to tears: of all who sat there, who wept the most? The Marshal of Jiangzhou—his blue gown wet through. Here the weeping pipa is Fourth Madam’s, and the grief it pours out is a twenty-year blood-feud. An allusion to that tradition, not a direct quotation.

Ximen Qing (西门庆) and Pan Jinlian (潘金莲) are the adulterous pair of the classic novels Water Margin (水浒传) and The Plum in the Golden Vase (金瓶梅): Pan, wife to the meek Wu Da, takes the rich rake Ximen Qing for her lover, and the two poison her husband to be rid of him. They are the standing byword in Chinese for a wife and her paramour who murder the husband—precisely the crime Fourth Madam lays at the door of her uncle and the concubine. Fiction, not history.

A ‘red-capped merchant’ (红顶商人) was a trader who also held official rank—the red button (顶戴) of a Qing mandarin worn atop the merchant’s hat—and so could do business under the protection and licence of the state. The type is epitomized by Hu Xueyan (胡雪岩, 1823–1885), the great financier of the late Qing. To make the murdered father such a merchant, and his wife the daughter of a secret-society chief, sets the family at the very crossing of official wealth and underworld power. Corroborated.

ch13.anchor: the Romance of the Three Kingdoms
ch13.note: The Romance of the Three Kingdoms (三国演义) is one of the four great classical Chinese novels, a sprawling historical epic of the wars that followed the fall of the Han, celebrated above all for its ruses, feints, and battles of wits. To call a scheme ‘the stalest trick out of the Three Kingdoms’ is to call it a stratagem every Chinese reader has met a hundred times. Corroborated.

Chinese deep mourning (披麻戴孝, ‘wearing hemp and mourning’) dressed the bereaved in coarse, undyed sackcloth of hemp or jute and unbleached white, the plainer and rougher the closer the kin—the opposite of Western black. The white banners, white flowers, and hemp robes here set a full funeral tableau before A-Chu. That it is staged for a father twenty years dead, to bind the son to revenge, is the scene's cold theatricality. Corroborated.

ch13.anchor: a long queue always trailed down
ch13.note: The queue (辫子)—the front of the head shaved and the rest grown long and braided—was imposed on Han Chinese men by the conquering Manchus in 1645 as the visible badge of submission to the Qing, on pain of death. By the last years of the dynasty it had become, to the reform-minded, a mark of servility and backwardness, and it was widely cut off after the revolution of 1911. The comedy of eunuchs waltzing in Western coats with queues swinging ‘like a tail’ is the collision of two worlds the whole novel watches. Corroborated.

‘Aunt-mother’ renders 姨娘, the name the children of a household used for their father’s concubine—a woman ranked below the wife (see the note on the Madams, Chapter 1) but addressed with the affection due a junior mother. The word marks her double place in the house: not the mother, yet a mother of sorts, and close in age here to the daughter who befriends her. Corroborated.

ch13.anchor: let the plum wither in the peach’s place
ch13.note: The image renders the set phrase 李代桃僵, ‘the plum dies in place of the peach.’ It comes from the Han yuefu ballad ‘Jiming,’ in which a plum growing beside a peach lets the insects gnaw its own roots and dies so the peach may live; it came to mean one person or thing sacrificed, or substituted, for another, and is the eleventh of the Thirty-Six Stratagems. Here the murdered Yang Yubo’s very name and place are taken over by the brother who killed him. Corroborated.

The bride-price (彩礼) was a gift of money and goods given by the groom’s family to the bride’s at betrothal—flowing opposite to a Western dowry, from the man’s side to the woman’s. Fourth Madam’s cover story turns on it: a destitute mother marrying off a daughter could raise a needed sum this way, which is exactly the pretext she uses to enter the Rong house. Corroborated.

ch14.note: The chapter title, 去时血漫桃源路 (‘when she went, blood ran red on the road to the peach-blossom spring’), turns Tao Yuanming’s (陶渊明, 365–427) famous fable The Record of the Peach Blossom Spring (桃花源记, c. 421) inside out. There a fisherman follows a stream lined with flowering peach trees to a hidden valley whose people, having fled the wars of an earlier age, live in perfect peace, walled off from the world’s strife; 桃源, ‘the peach-blossom source,’ has been the Chinese byword ever since for an untouched refuge. The line makes that refuge run with blood: the hospital where A-Chu meant to take ship for a free life becomes instead a field of slaughter. The allusion is corroborated; the bloody inversion is the novelist’s own.

A-Chu measures himself against a maxim of Mencius (孟子, 4th c. BCE), from Exhausting the Mind I: ‘in want, keep your own self good; come to greatness, and make the whole world good besides’ (穷则独善其身，达则兼善天下). To ‘keep one’s own self good’ (独善其身) is to hold one’s integrity intact when one cannot mend the world; A-Chu’s despair is that even this last, least virtue is now being stripped from him. Corroborated.

ch14.anchor: cut the flesh from his own thigh
ch14.note: The Fourth Madam’s taunt invokes 割股疗亲, ‘cutting the flesh of one’s own thigh to heal a parent’—the extreme of filial devotion, in which a child boils a slice of his own flesh into medicine for a dying elder. A stock motif of the dynastic literature of filial exemplars, it stands here for the doctor (and the son) who will give his own body for those to whom he owes his life; she is saying A-Chu is no such doctor. Corroborated as a traditional motif.

ch14.anchor: wiped out by his very hand
ch14.note: The Chinese (她要自己亲手除去这一对狗男女) is grammatically ambiguous: the reflexive 自己 (‘oneself’) attaches to the sentence’s subject, the Fourth Madam, so the line can be read ‘she wanted to wipe them out with her own hand.’ Yet her whole scheme, stated plainly elsewhere, is that the killing must be done by Yang blood—by A-Chu—while she only looks on; the speech just above says as much (‘I want you to kill them with your own hands’). We render the sense the plot requires and flag the looseness rather than smooth it over.

The source names this character inconsistently — 汤少礼 (Tang Shaoli) here and 汤少棋 (Tang Shaoqi) later in the same chapter — evidently a slip for one and the same man; each spelling is kept where it stands, and the bare 汤少 is rendered ‘Young Tang.’

ch14.anchor: To save the world and ferry men across
ch14.note: A-Chu’s creed, 救世渡人, borrows a Buddhist image: du (渡/度) is to ferry living beings across the sea of suffering to the far shore of release, the work of a bodhisattva. He turns it to a doctor’s vocation of healing and rescue, which is why he sets it flatly against killing: to ferry men across and to cut them down are opposite motions. Corroborated.

‘Building the Great Wall’ (砌长城) is the standing jest for a game of mahjong: at the start the tiles are stacked face down into four long walls that the players demolish as they draw, so a table of mahjong looks like four little Great Walls going up. The Madams are at their tiles, the commonest pastime of a leisured household. Corroborated.

ch14.anchor: Qin by morning and Chu by nightfall
ch14.note: The taunt renders 朝秦暮楚, ‘serve Qin in the morning, Chu by evening.’ In the Warring States era small states shifted allegiance between the rival powers Qin and Chu as advantage dictated; the phrase became the byword for one who changes sides or lovers without constancy. Young Tang is sneering that He Yashu is fickle in her affections and so has no right to feel slighted. Corroborated.

The Green Gang (青帮) and Red Gang (红帮, or 洪帮) were the great secret-society brotherhoods of Republican Shanghai, part fraternal order and part criminal syndicate, controlling the docks, opium, and protection rackets and reaching deep into business and politics; the Green Gang under Du Yuesheng was the most powerful. To ask whether A-Chu has offended them is to ask whether the bombing was underworld work. Corroborated.

ch14.anchor: the road to the Yellow Springs
ch14.note: The Yellow Springs (黄泉, huangquan) are the Chinese land of the dead, a shadowy realm deep beneath the earth to which the soul descends—the road there is the road into death. The narrator wonders whether Fourth Madam, now dead, found in that world the vengeance she never won in this one. Corroborated.

ch15.anchor: how high the source once lay
ch15.note: The chapter title, 到底方知出处高 (‘only in the end do you know how high the source lies’), is the second line of the poem A-Chu writes back to Rong Sheng on his fan, which reworks a celebrated Tang quatrain on a waterfall, the Linked Verses on the Waterfall (瀑布联句): through a thousand crags and ten thousand ravines it grudges no toil; only seen from afar do you know how high its source lies; how could the brooks and gorges ever hold it back?—in the end it reaches the great sea and becomes the breakers. Tradition makes it a joint work: the opening couplet by a Chan monk, the close by Li Chen (李忱), the future Emperor Xuanzong of Tang (r. 846–859), then living in obscurity. The novel credits the monk as Xiangyan (香严); scholarship more often names Huangbo Xiyun (黄檗希运), with Xiangyan a competing ascription—the poem is genuine and Tang, the monastic attribution disputed. Despite the echoing ‘方知…高,’ this is a different poem from Du Xunhe’s The Little Pine quoted at Chapter 5: A-Chu’s waterfall, unlike the unrecognized pine, already knows its own height and is bound for the sea.

ch15.anchor: fire of sin comes down like thunder
ch15.note: This second passage from the phonograph is the other half of the aria footnoted at Chapter 12—the song of Jiao Guiying (敫桂英) from The Ardent Probe (情探), the stage version of the old tale Wang Kui Betrays Guiying (王魁负桂英). There the courtesan, cast off by the scholar she once raised to office, takes her own life and returns a ghost to drag him across the border of yin and yang and exact the debt of her death (孽火…拉入阴阳界，索还命债). At Chapter 12 the Fourth Madam herself sang the earlier verse, and A-Chu felt a chill run to his marrow; now she lies in the coffin the record plays before, and the song’s wronged, self-slain woman, come back for blood, has been made flesh in her own end. Corroborated.

ch15.anchor: the three knives and the six holes
ch15.note: ‘Three knives and six holes’ (三刀六洞) is a penance of the Jianghu brotherhoods: a member who has broken faith submits to being run through three times, each thrust leaving an entry and an exit wound—three knives, six holes—paying the debt off with his own blood and body. In offering to ‘spare’ Han Zhengqi the three knives and six holes, A-Chu already speaks as the head of the society, holding the old man’s life in his hand. A recognized secret-society usage.

ch15.anchor: the principal mother and the mother who bore her
ch15.note: In a polygynous house the principal wife’s children ranked as 嫡 (of the main line) and a concubine’s as 庶 (shuchu, ‘of the branch’), lower in standing and inheritance (see the note on the Madams, Chapter 1). Yet every child formally called the principal wife ‘mother’—the 嫡母 or ritual mother—while the concubine who actually bore them was the 生母, the birth mother. Ronghua, borne by the Third Madam, is thus torn between the First Madam she must honor and the mother of her own blood; and it is because Rongrong is concubine-born that the First Madam holds her funeral of small account. Corroborated.

ch15.anchor: Books of loyalty and filial piety, of honor and righteousness
ch15.note: Loyalty, filial piety, honor, and righteousness (忠孝节义) are the four cardinal virtues of Confucian popular morality and the stock themes of the operas and storybooks on which a traditional child was raised. That Rong Chu was schooled on such books frames the fierce sense of filial duty—and of vengeance owed a parent—that drives him. Corroborated.

ch15.anchor: ridden off on the yellow crane
ch15.note: The image alludes to Cui Hao’s (崔颢, d. 754) celebrated Tang poem ‘Yellow Crane Tower’ (黄鹤楼), whose opening—the one of old has ridden off on the yellow crane, and here remains only the empty tower—became the classic elegy for someone gone beyond recall. The narrator turns it on the dead Fourth Madam: she who is gone has ridden the yellow crane away, and here only an endless grief remains. Corroborated.

ch15.anchor: the endless, unbroken wars of the warlords
ch15.note: After Yuan Shikai’s death in 1916 China fragmented among rival militarists, and roughly a decade of shifting warlord wars (军阀混战) followed until the Nationalists’ nominal reunification in 1928. Han Zhengqi’s soldiering years fall in that chaos, the violence he wearied of before drifting to Shanghai. Corroborated.

A ‘master-pledge card’ renders 拜师帖, the written pledge by which one performs 拜师—kneeling and kowtowing to acknowledge a master—and so binds oneself as his disciple. In the secret-society world such a pledge sealed a lifelong bond of obedience and protection between master and man; Han Zhengqi’s old card, sworn to the Golden Dragon Society, is what A-Chu—now its head—holds out to reclaim his allegiance. Corroborated.

ch16.note: At this point, and again twice at the dinner table below (‘A-Chu set down the silver spoon’; ‘Which company has the Yang family’s bank worked with…’), the source prints 杨慕次 (Yang Muci), the spy-school twin, where the scene is plainly his brother 杨慕初 / 阿初 (Yang Muchu / A-Chu): Muci is away in Hangzhou sitting his final examination throughout this chapter and cannot be in the Shanghai garden or at the Rong dinner table. The twins’ given names differ by a single character (次 / 初), and the slip is almost certainly authorial or typographical; it is rendered here by context (Muchu / A-Chu) and flagged rather than silently reconciled.

ch16.anchor: drove Scholar Zhang out of his wits
ch16.note: Rong Chu is humming a line from The Romance of the Western Chamber (西厢记), the Yuan-dynasty music-drama by Wang Shifu (王实甫, c. 1250–1300): 则为他临去秋波那一转，风魔了张解元. ‘Scholar Zhang’ (张解元) is the student Zhang Sheng (张生), the play’s hero, whom a single parting glance from Cui Yingying leaves lovesick; 解元 is the title of the man placed first in the provincial examinations. The line reworks Zhang’s own famous cry in the first act, 怎当他临去秋波那一转 (‘how could I withstand that one turn of her autumn glance as she went’); Rong Chu sings the paraphrase current in the sung tanci (弹词) storytelling tradition, which Young Tang at once forbids him.

The September 18th Incident (九一八事变), also called the Mukden Incident, of 1931: on the night of 18 September the Kwantung Army staged a bombing on the South Manchuria Railway near Shenyang (Mukden) and used it as a pretext to occupy Manchuria — the ‘Three Eastern Provinces’ (东三省) of Liaoning, Jilin, and Heilongjiang — within months, setting up the puppet state of Manchukuo in 1932. It touched off the nationwide boycott of Japanese goods that is the backdrop to A-Chu’s anger here, and it fixes the chapter’s present after the autumn of 1931, consistent with the 1932 newspaper notices later in the chapter.

ch16.anchor: how does that make a man less a man
ch16.note: A-Chu quotes the second line of Lu Xun’s (鲁迅, 1881–1936) quatrain In Answer to a Guest’s Jest (答客诮): 无情未必真豪杰，怜子如何不丈夫 (‘the heartless are not surely the true heroes; to cherish one’s child — how does that make a man less a man?’). Lu Xun wrote it on 31 December 1932, rebuking those who had mocked his fondness for his infant son; the whole poem is a defense of a father’s tenderness. In A-Chu’s mouth, as he watches the bird’s nest, it turns cold: he has just used that very tenderness — Han Zhengqi’s love for his son Han Yu — as the lever by which to bind the father to him.

The chapter title, 山回路转又逢君 (‘the hills wind, the road turns, and I meet you again’), inverts the closing couplet of Cen Shen’s (岑参, c. 715–770) Song of White Snow, Seeing Off Assistant Magistrate Wu on His Return to the Capital (白雪歌送武判官归京): 山回路转不见君，雪上空留马行处 (‘the hills wind, the road turns, and I see you no more; only the tracks of your horse are left on the snow’), one of the most celebrated farewells in Tang poetry, a parting on a snowbound frontier. Zhang Yong turns Cen Shen’s ‘I see you no more’ (不见君) into ‘I meet you again’ (又逢君): the chapter’s winding mountain roads end not in separation but in Ronghua’s ‘Welcome home’ to Yang Muci, a reunion of comrades in place of a leave-taking. The allusion is corroborated; the couplet is Cen Shen’s, from a poem securely in the Tang canon.

ch16.anchor: A wild goose’s claw leaves its mark in the snow
ch16.note: Yang Muchu turns a famous image of Su Shi (苏轧, 1037–1101), the great Song poet: 人生到处知何似，应似飞鸿踏雪泥—‘to what may a life be likened, wherever it goes? Surely to a wild goose treading the snow-mud, that leaves the chance print of its claws before it flies on, careless of east or west’ (On the Snow at Mianchi, in Answer to Ziyou, 1061). The image, 雪泥鸿爪, became the stock phrase for the faint, accidental traces the past leaves behind. A-Chu means that Young Tang, for all his professed heartlessness, must somewhere carry the mark of an old love. Corroborated.

ch16.anchor: seven or eight hundred million fabi
ch16.note: Fabi (法币, ‘legal tender’) was the paper currency the Nationalist government made China’s sole legal money in the currency reform of November 1935, taking the country off the silver standard and calling in privately held silver. The term is used a little ahead of its time in this 1932 scene, loosely for the national paper currency; the point is simply that the Dongyang Company’s sales run to hundreds of millions. Corroborated.

A comprador (买办, maiban; the word is Portuguese for ‘buyer’) was the Chinese manager who ran a foreign firm’s business in the treaty ports—its go-between with local merchants, banks, and officials. Grown rich as the indispensable middlemen of foreign trade, the compradors became a byword in nationalist and Marxist rhetoric for a native bourgeoisie that served imperial capital against China’s own interest, which is exactly the contempt A-Chu loads into the phrase. Corroborated.

ch16.anchor: the Eight-Nation Alliance stormed and took Peking
ch16.note: In the summer of 1900 an army of eight foreign powers—Britain, the United States, France, Germany, Russia, Japan, Italy, and Austria-Hungary—marched on the capital to break the siege of the foreign legations during the Boxer Uprising, and in August took and sacked Peking, driving the Qing court into flight. The campaign, and the punitive looting that followed, became a lasting emblem of national humiliation at foreign hands—A-Chu’s bitter point that superior ‘science and technology,’ born of Chinese gunpowder, was turned against China itself. Corroborated.

ch17.note: The chapter title, 各有经缝一片天 (‘each has a sky of its own warp and weft’), is not a traceable classical quotation but a couplet in the old manner supplied by the author, and is rendered here literally. 经缝 (jingwei) is the warp and weft of weaving, and by extension the ordering of affairs, the threads by which a scheme is run — the same image Xu Yuzhen turns on Han Zhengqi here (经缝万端, ‘the threads of warp and weft run to a thousand ends’) and which returns when the three antagonists sit down face to face, each ‘nursing designs of his own’ (各怀经缝). The title’s point is that each party to the confrontation weaves a private world of intrigue beneath one shared sky.

The September 18th Incident (九·一八事变), known in the West as the Mukden Incident: on 18 September 1931 officers of Japan’s Kwantung Army staged an explosion on the South Manchuria Railway near Shenyang (Mukden) and used it as a pretext to seize the city and, within months, all of Manchuria. Chiang Kai-shek’s Nationalist government ordered ‘absolute non-resistance,’ and Japan set up the puppet state of Manchukuo the following year. The account here is historically accurate.

Doihara Kenji (土肥原跴二, 1883–1948) was a real Japanese Army officer and spymaster, for decades the chief of Japanese military intelligence in China; after the war the Tokyo tribunal convicted him as a Class-A war criminal and he was hanged in 1948. The likening of women agents to ‘cherry blossoms’ drifting onto the mainland belongs to the novel. The ‘Liyang Society’ (立洋社) and its ‘Eastern Institute’ (东洋学馆) on Kunshan Road are not attested under those names in the historical record and appear to be the book’s invention, though they echo the real use of Japanese-run ‘institutes’ and trading houses in Shanghai as covers for intelligence work.

Lu Yu (陆羽, 733–804), honored as the Sage of Tea (茶圣) for his Classic of Tea (茶经), the first treatise on the subject. The six lines A-Chu recites are Lu Yu’s own Song of Six Longings (六羽歌), one of only two of his poems to survive; the ‘waters of the West River’ and ‘Jingling’ name the river and the town of his childhood home, in present-day Tianmen, Hubei. The quotation is accurate.

ch17.anchor: we sprang, the two of us, from the selfsame root
ch17.note: These four lines are the famous Seven-Step Poem (七步诗) attributed to Cao Zhi (曹植, 192–232). By tradition his brother Cao Pi, the new emperor, ordered him to compose a poem in the time it took to walk seven paces, on pain of death, and Cao Zhi answered with these lines on beans boiled over a fire of their own stalks — brother destroying brother though both are of one root. A-Chu quotes it for plain reason: the whole book turns on twin brothers set against each other, and on kin who murder kin.

ch17.anchor: ran a deliberately strange, sidelong gaze over her
ch17.note: Here, and here only in this chapter, the source prints 杨慕次 (Yang Muci), the spy-school twin, where the speaker is plainly his brother 杨慕初 / 阿初 (Yang Muchu / A-Chu): the whole tearoom confrontation is A-Chu’s, and he has given his own name as Yang Muchu only a few lines above. The twins’ names differ by a single character (次 / 初), and the slip — recurring from the previous chapter — is almost certainly authorial or typographical; it is rendered here by context and flagged rather than silently reconciled. The familiar name 阿次 / A-Ci, by contrast, is genuinely Muci’s.

The Special Higher Police (特高科, from Japanese Tokkō, 特別高等警察) were Japan’s political and secret police, founded in 1911 to hunt down dissidents, radicals, and foreign agents; branches followed the empire’s expansion into Korea, Taiwan, and the areas it penetrated in China. Here they are the counter-intelligence arm from whose hands the Communist agents have lifted the photographed Japanese survey maps. Corroborated.

ch17.anchor: Secretary of the Central Special Branch
ch17.note: The Central Special Branch (中央特科, the Teke) was the Chinese Communist Party’s clandestine security and intelligence service, set up in Shanghai in 1927 and directed in its early years by Zhou Enlai. It gathered intelligence, penetrated the police and rival services, and ran a ‘Red Squad’ that assassinated traitors and protected the underground leadership; it answered to the Party’s Special Committee (中央特委), the ‘enlarged meeting’ of which the Comintern delegate is coming to attend. The defection of its chief of operations, Gu Shunzhang, in 1931 had lately dealt it a devastating blow. Corroborated.

The Hongmen (洪门, ‘Vast Gate’) was a sprawling Chinese sworn-brotherhood tradition descended from the anti-Manchu secret societies of the Qing, kin to the Triads and to the overseas ‘Chinese Freemasons’; by the Republican era its lodges ran deep through the gangs, the police, and the commerce of a city like Shanghai. That Huang Sanyuan is at once a senior French-Concession detective and the Hongmen’s chief — ‘a foot in both the black road and the white’ — is exactly the fusion of underworld and authority the society is invoked for. Corroborated.

ch17.anchor: the red apricot bough stray over the wall
ch17.note: ‘The red apricot straying over the wall’ (红杏出墙) is the stock Chinese image for a wife’s adultery. It descends from a Song couplet by Ye Shaoweng (叶绍翁), ‘the garden’s spring cannot be shut in — a spray of red apricot reaches out over the wall,’ whose blossom escaping the enclosure came to stand for a woman straying from her husband. Huang Sanyuan is citing the Hongmen’s code: the adulterer struck by Heaven’s thunder, the adulterous wife cut down by the blade. Corroborated.

These four words — wa, kei, sei, jaku (和敬清寄) — are the canonical four principles of the Japanese Way of tea, by tradition distilled by the great tea master Sen no Rikyū (千利休, 1522–1591): harmony between guests and things, reverence for others, purity of heart and setting, and the tranquility that the first three yield. Xu Yuzhen invokes them as the discipline she has mastered; A-Chu’s retort is that Chinese tea seeks instead the ‘oneness of Heaven and man.’ Corroborated.

ch17.anchor: Lord Guan patrolling the city wall
ch17.note: ‘Lord Guan patrolling the city wall’ (关公巡城) and ‘Han Xin numbering his troops’ (韩信点兵) are the set names of two motions in Chaozhou-style gongfu tea: pouring in swift circles round the ranked cups so that all fill evenly, then dealing out the last strong drops one cup at a time so none is slighted. They borrow the names of two famous generals — Guan Yu (关羽), the god of war of the Three Kingdoms, and Han Xin (韩信), the great strategist of the founding of the Han. A-Chu’s flawless performance of them is his proof that the art of tea is Chinese. Corroborated.

ch17.anchor: opened the incense hall and swore themselves brothers
ch17.note: To ‘pay respects at the wharf’ (拜码头) was for a newcomer to present himself, and a gift, to the local boss on entering his territory; to ‘open the incense hall’ (开香堂) and swear brotherhood (拜把子) was the secret societies’ solemn rite of the sworn brother, sealed before burning incense and the gods, by which unrelated men became kin bound to stand by one another for life. By these two acts A-Chu buys his way into the Shanghai underworld and binds Huang Sanyuan to him. Corroborated.

ch18.anchor: out of the tangled and disordered threads
ch18.note: The chapter title, 牵丝攀藤一条线 (‘drawing the silk, climbing the vine, a single thread’), plays on the set phrase 牵丝攀藤, to drag in far-fetched or tenuous connections. The phrase is ordinarily disparaging (‘pulling east and attaching west’), but the title turns it to A-Chu’s method in this chapter, in which he draws every stray, tenuous clue together into one continuous thread of deduction. It is not a classical quotation but a couplet in the old manner supplied by the author, and is rendered here literally.

ch18.anchor: and to be without heirs is the greatest
ch18.note: A-Chu quotes one of the most famous sayings of Mencius (孟子, 4th c. BCE): 不孝有三，无后为大 — ‘there are three unfilial things, and to have no heir is the greatest of them.’ In the classic scheme of filial piety, a man’s first duty is to continue his father’s line, for only a son can carry on the sacrifices at the ancestral altar; to die without a male heir is to let the family’s ‘incense-fire’ (香火) go out and abandon the ancestors. This is why the Empress Dowager’s gift of a concubine to beget a son is, in the logic A-Chu reconstructs, an act of favor and not of cruelty. Corroborated; the enumeration of the ‘three’ is the Han commentator Zhao Qi’s.

ch18.anchor: keep a fast and fulfill a vow
ch18.note: To ‘keep a fast’ (吃斩, chizhai) is to take up the Buddhist abstinence from meat, and to ‘fulfill a vow’ (还愿, huanyuan) is to return to a temple to make the offering one promised a god or bodhisattva in exchange for a granted wish. A retreat of some days at a temple for these devotions was an ordinary act of piety for a woman of the household; the sinister point here is that it gave the plotters their chance, the birth mother murdered and replaced during just such a stay at the Ciyun Temple. Corroborated.

ch19.anchor: a row of last plum trees
ch19.note: The chapter title, 梅花一夜漏春工 (‘in a single night the plum blossom betrays spring’s craft’), is not a traceable classical quotation but a seven-character line in the old manner supplied by the author, and is rendered here literally. It works within a long poetic tradition—widened by Wang Anshi (王安石)—in which the early plum ‘leaks’ or ‘betrays’ (漏, 漏泄) the news of a spring not yet arrived. The image fits the chapter: in one night A-Chu’s long-hidden self begins to show through—Xin Lili and Cong Feng each take him for his twin, and the Comintern delegate is quietly brought in—as the plum gives away the coming season before its time.

Yu Xuanji (鱼玄机, c. 844–871) was a celebrated Tang-dynasty woman poet, famous for her beauty and her verse and long remembered as a courtesan-poet; A-Chu cites her to argue that a woman of the ‘blue houses’ need not be a wanton. Historically she entered a Daoist convent, not the ‘Buddhist gate’ the source names here (遁入佛门), so that detail is contradicted by the record, though the figure herself is real. 艳帜高张, rendered ‘flew her gaudy flag as high as any,’ means to be renowned as a great beauty.

The 月份牌 (‘calendar poster’) was a form of commercial art peculiar to Republican-era Shanghai: an advertising calendar printed by color lithography, typically showing a fashionable modern beauty or a dapper young gentleman, given away by companies to promote their wares. To liken Cong Feng to a figure on one is to call him decorative and a little unreal.

ch19.anchor: the eldest brother stands as a father
ch19.note: A-Chu invokes the old maxim 长兄如父，长娄比母 and its like: within the Confucian family the eldest son, once the father is dead, holds a father’s authority over his younger siblings, who owe him a father’s obedience. By this rule A-Chu — the elder twin and lawful heir — claims the right to command his brother Yang Muci, whatever Muci’s own standing. The principle ranks brothers strictly by age, and it is the ground of the whole contest of wills between the twins. Corroborated.

ch19.anchor: When I play at opera, I am furthering the national essence
ch19.note: To ‘play at opera’ (票戏) was the pastime of the well-born amateur (票友) who studied and performed Peking opera for love of the art rather than for pay; a leisured young gentleman’s command of the arias was a mark of cultivation. The ‘national essence’ (国粹, guocui) was the period’s honorific for Peking opera and the other traditional arts held to embody the quintessence of Chinese culture. Young Tang’s joke is to dignify his idle dilettantism as patriotic guardianship of that heritage — and then to strain the same excuse to cover his opium. Corroborated.

ch20.anchor: the smile of friends long parted and met again
ch20.note: The chapter title, 一笑相逢哪易得 (‘a meeting met with a smile is not easily won’), is a seven-character line in the old manner supplied by the author, rendered here literally; it is not a traceable single classical quotation, though the phrase 一笑相逢 (‘to meet with a single smile’) is a stock one in Song lyric, as in Zhou Bangyan’s (周邦彦) Die lian hua: ‘一笑相逢蓬海路’. The chapter turns on two such hard-won meetings—the reunion of A-Chu and his old friend Cong Feng, and the first face-to-face of the estranged twins.

A-Chu is needling Cong Feng about where he has really come from. 大海啊，你这自由的元素 renders the apostrophe to the sea in Pushkin’s To the Sea (‘K moryu,’ 1824), commonly Englished ‘Farewell, free element!’; a few lines on, ‘the insulted and the injured’ (被侮辱与损害的) is the title of Dostoevsky’s novel of 1861. Both are Russian touchstones A-Chu drops to signal, under Ronghua’s ear, that the delegate comes from the Soviet Union.

ch20.anchor: There is no water that does not run downward
ch20.note: A-Ci is quoting Mencius (孟子, Gaozi I): 人无有不善，水无有不下—‘there is no man who is not good, and no water that does not run downward,’ the classic argument that human nature is innately good, as water naturally flows down. He turns it on A-Chu to insist there must be some good reason behind the extortion.

Here, and in the dialogue that follows, the source prints the borrowed name in quotation marks, ‘杨羽柏’ (‘Yang Yubo’), and then reverts to the man’s true name, 杨羽桦 (Yang Yuhua). They are one and the same person in the novel’s present: Yang Yuhua, the Yang family’s second master, murdered his elder brother—the real Yang Yubo, Muci’s father—and, being alike in looks, took over his identity, his wealth and his wife (revealed in Chapters 12 to 14). He is rendered here by context and the doubling flagged, not silently reconciled.

ch20.anchor: a grown man of seven feet
ch20.note: The Chinese 尺 (chi), conventionally Englished ‘foot,’ is shorter than the English foot, so 七尺 (‘seven chi’) describes not a giant but a man of ordinary adult height. 七尺男儿 and 七尺之躯 are stock phrases for an able-bodied grown man, carrying the sense of a person of full stature and the dignity proper to one. A-Ci’s indignation is that of a grown man told to hold out his hand to his parents for money. Corroborated.

The Dragon King (龙王) is the folk water-god who commands rain, rivers, and the sea, his temples a fixture of old Chinese towns. Cong Feng is quoting a two-part folk saying, 大水冲了龙王庙，一家人不认一家人 (‘the flood has washed away the Dragon King’s own temple: kinfolk no longer knowing their own kin’), used when people of one side clash by mistake before recognizing that they belong together. Learning that A-Chu and Ronghua are of one household, he means that they have been at cross-purposes like the flood and the god’s own shrine. Corroborated.

The 策论 (‘policy dissertation’) was the essay on statecraft a candidate wrote in answer to set questions in the imperial examinations, the graded state tests that from the Sui and Tang dynasties to 1905 were the sole ladder into the scholar-official class. A-Chu’s 举子 who ‘leap the Dragon Gate’ are the successful candidates, likened to the carp of legend that leaps the gorge of the Yellow River and is transformed into a dragon. His point is that a civilization schooled for centuries to declaim fixed positions on command never learned to converse as equals. Corroborated.

‘Ears-that-hear-on-the-wind’ (顺风耳) and its partner ‘Thousand-li Eyes’ (千里眼) are folk deities, the sharp-eared and sharp-eyed guardians who attend the sea-goddess Mazu; the pair are proverbial for beings who hear and see everything, however far off. Finding that Rong Chu has somehow overheard the whole conversation, A-Chu dubs him the all-hearing one. Corroborated.

ch21.anchor: a bolt from a clear sky
ch21.note: The chapter title, 千钧一发箭在弦 (‘a thousandweight on a hair, the arrow on the string’), gathers two classical figures for a danger poised to break at a touch. 千钧一发 is from the Tang writer Han Yu (韩愈), Letter to Meng Jian (与孟尚书书): 其危如一发引千钧, ‘the peril of it, as a single hair drawing a thousand jun.’ 箭在弦上 is from Chen Lin (陈琳), whose words survive as 矢在弦上，不得不发, ‘the arrow on the string cannot but be loosed.’ Both are corroborated. The novel’s own title, 一触即发 (‘one touch and it goes off,’ said first of a drawn bow—hence On a Hair Trigger), is the same image; and it is here, with the Party’s whole network suddenly poised to fall into enemy hands, that the tension is drawn to its fullest.

老向 (‘Old Xiang’), and below 向先生 / 向书记 (‘Mr. Xiang’ / ‘Secretary Xiang’), are the underground cover-name of Fang Zhitong (方致同), Secretary of the Central Special Branch: comrades address him as Xiang, and so do his captors. All refer to the same man, named in full by the narration as Fang Zhitong.
