ch22.anchor: blocking the vital artery to Hengji Li
ch22.note: The chapter title, 截断众流大气魄 (‘to dam all the currents takes a vast resolve’), turns on the Chan phrase 截断众流 (‘cut off the myriad streams’), one of the ‘three phrases of Yunmen’ (云门三句) attributed to the Tang–Song Chan master Yunmen Wenyan (云门文偃): the other two are 涵盖乾坤 and 随波逐流. As a complete seven-character line the title is not a traceable quotation but the author’s own pastiche in the old manner (like the titles of Chapters 17, 19 and 20); the borrowed Chan figure of ‘damming every stream’ is fitted to Ronghua’s act, which literally dams the flow of both traffic and comrades pouring toward the trap.

ch22.anchor: Gu Shunzhang was a member of the Party’s Central Committee
ch22.note: Gu Shunzhang (顾顺章, 1904–1935) really was the head of the Communist Special Branch’s security and ‘Red Squad’ (红队) and a Central Committee member. Arrested in Wuhan in April 1931, he defected at once, threatening to destroy the whole Shanghai underground. The catastrophe was averted because Qian Zhuangfei (钱壮飞), a Communist mole inside the Nationalists’ own cipher office, intercepted the warning telegrams and got word to the leadership, which relocated its organs overnight—exactly the ‘one coded telegram, and in a single night the Communists vanished’ that Adjutant Liu describes. The account here is corroborated by the historical record.

ch22.anchor: Wu Hao—the highest man in charge
ch22.note: ‘Mr. Wu’ / Wu Hao (伍豪) is a documented alias of Zhou Enlai (周恩来), who in this period directed the Communist Party’s Special Branch (特科) in Shanghai. The pseudonym is corroborated; it became notorious in 1932 through the forged ‘Wu Hao notices’ (伍豪启事) planted in the Shanghai press to announce his supposed defection. That the amah expects ‘Mr. Wu’ in person marks how close the raid comes to the very top of the apparatus.

The source here writes 荣华书店 (‘Ronghua Bookstore,’ after its proprietor), whereas everywhere else—including the next chapter—the same shop is named 华美书店, the Huamei Bookstore. The inconsistency is the author’s; both name the one shop, and it is rendered here as the text stands rather than silently reconciled.

The shikumen (石库门, ‘stone-gate’) is the characteristic Shanghai row house of the concession era, a brick terrace dwelling entered through a heavy stone door-frame and ranged along narrow interior lanes (弄堂, longtang). With doors front and rear giving onto a warren of connected alleys, such houses suited the Communist underground exactly: lookouts could watch every approach, and members could slip out the back at the first sign of danger — which is precisely how the meeting-house here is meant to work. Corroborated.

ch22.anchor: the stout fellows of Liangshan Marsh
ch22.note: Liangshan Marsh (梁山泊) is the marsh-ringed mountain stronghold of the hundred and eight outlaw heroes of the classic novel Water Margin (水浒传), the standing Chinese byword for bravos of unbreakable toughness and sworn brotherhood. Xiong Zida means that not even those legendary hard men could hold out under his instruments of torture; the ‘108’ of his boast in the same breath is itself the outlaws’ number. Corroborated.

ch23.anchor: the very grass and trees seemed to stink of blood
ch23.note: The chapter title, 恶氛弥天血火焚 (‘a foul miasma fills the sky; blood and fire consume’), is the author’s own seven-character line rather than a traceable quotation, rendered here literally. 草木皆腥 (‘even the grass and trees smell of blood’) plays on the set phrase 草木皆兵 (‘every bush and tree looks like an enemy soldier’), from the rout at the Fei River (淝水之战, 383) recorded in the Book of Jin (晋书): the author swaps 兵 (‘soldiers’) for 腥 (‘the reek of blood’) to fit the carnage of the crash.

Rh-negative blood is genuinely rare among Han Chinese—on the order of three in a thousand, as the text says (千分之三), against roughly fifteen in a hundred among people of European descent—so a shared Rh-negative type A is a strong, if not conclusive, sign of kinship. The novel uses it as the physical proof of what the twins do not yet openly acknowledge: it is A-Chu’s stored plasma that saves A-Ci, and the mingling of their blood that first stirs A-Chu’s sense of a brother.

ch23.anchor: the plane trees along the great street
ch23.note: The plane trees (法国梧桐, literally ‘French wutong’) are the London planes the French planted along the avenues of their Shanghai concession from the early years of the century; their broad, mottled shade became, and remains, the emblem of the old foreign quarters of the city. Corroborated.

ch24.anchor: a grieving wind fills the road
ch24.note: The chapter title, 风雨未肯收余寒 (‘the wind and rain will not yet give up the lingering cold’), is the author’s own line in the classical manner rather than a traceable quotation; the figure of a late cold that will not lift echoes the stock poetic 余寒 (‘lingering cold’) of early-spring verse. It is rendered here literally. A-Chu’s coded message—悲风满路, ‘a grieving wind fills the road’—carries the same weather into the warning he sends A-Ci.

‘Daiyu burns her manuscripts’ (黛玉焚稿) is the celebrated episode in Chapter 97 of Dream of the Red Chamber (红楼梦): Lin Daiyu (林黛玉), betrayed in love and dying, burns the poems and handkerchiefs that hold her heart. The First Madam’s remark is corroborated as an allusion to that scene, and doubles as a grim foreshadowing—Ronghua is said to have inherited not only Daiyu’s gifts but her ill-starred, early-cut fate.

ch24.anchor: better to kill a thousand by mistake than let one slip through
ch24.note: 宁可错杀一千，也不放过一个 (‘better to kill a thousand by mistake than let one slip through’), with its cruder twin 宁枉勿纵 (‘wrong the innocent rather than let the guilty go’), is the notorious slogan of the Nationalist ‘White Terror’ that followed the anti-Communist purge of 1927. It is genuinely documented as a watchword of that repression, though its exact origin is disputed and it is only traditionally—not verifiably—put in Chiang Kai-shek’s own mouth; Yu Xiaojiang here cites it as the Generalissimo’s standing instruction.

The pairing is from the classic novel Journey to the West (西游记): the resourceful 孙悟空 (Sun Wukong, the Monkey King) against the plodding 沙和尚 (Sha Wujing, here ‘Sha Monk’) — a capable troublemaker reckoned better than a harmless dullard.

ch25.anchor: to step backward was, all along, to go forward
ch25.note: The chapter title, 退步原来是向前 (‘to step backward was, all along, to go forward’), is the closing line of the 《插秧诗》 (‘Rice-Planting Song’), a Chan quatrain attributed to the Cloth-Bag Monk (布袋和尚), Qici (契此), traditionally placed in the Five Dynasties. The received text runs 手把青秧插满田，低头便见水中天，六根清净方为道，退步原来是向前 (‘green shoots in hand, he fills the paddy field; head bowed, he sees the sky within the water; only when the six senses are pure is it the Way; to step back was, all along, to go forward’). A-Chu quotes it almost verbatim, though the novel gives a variant third line (顺其自然方是道, ‘to go along with nature is the Way’) and misplaces it in the ‘former Tang.’ The attribution to Budai is corroborated as the traditional one, the poem being among the best known of Chan verses.

ch25.anchor: grafting of one flower upon another
ch25.note: 移花接木 (‘to graft one flower onto another tree’) is a set phrase for a covert substitution, swapping the true for the false so that no seam shows. Here it names A-Chu and Xia Yuechun’s ruse: a look-alike is presented as the injured Yang Muci first, so that Li Qinhong’s men, having fixed his identity by sight, never think to scrutinize the real man’s voice.

ch25.anchor: what the ear hears is empty; what the eye sees is real
ch25.note: 耳听为虚，眼见为实 (‘what the ear hears is empty; what the eye sees is real’) is a common proverb asserting the primacy of sight over hearsay. Xia Yuechun turns it into the very principle of the deception: because the visual cue has already answered the question, his listeners discount the auditory one—precisely the blind spot the substitution exploits.

ch26.anchor: In advancing, no joy; in retreating, no grief
ch26.note: A-Chu’s answer, 进亦不喜，退亦不忧 (‘in advancing, no joy; in retreating, no grief’), inverts the famous antithesis of Fan Zhongyan’s 《岳阳楼记》 (‘Record of the Yueyang Tower,’ 1046), 是进亦忧，退亦忧 (‘thus he grieves whether he advances or retreats’), and echoes its 不以物喜，不以己悲 (‘he takes no joy in outward things, no sorrow in himself’). The allusion is corroborated; A-Chu recasts Fan’s selfless statesman as a portrait of a woman’s equanimity, and hears it, rightly, as a likeness of Yashu.

ch26.anchor: Bai Yun was Tian Xiuyun’s alias
ch26.note: The chapter title, 白云可杀不可留 (‘the white cloud may be slain but not detained’), is the author’s own seven-character line in the classical manner rather than a traceable quotation; no earlier source has been found for it (uncorroborated). It puns on 白云, at once the ‘white cloud,’ that drifting emblem of a free and unfettered spirit, and Bai Yun, the alias of the courier Tian Xiuyun, whose old recantation surfaces here to mark her, in the organization’s eyes, for death.

ch26.anchor: you wear out iron shoes tramping in search of it
ch26.note: 踏破铁鞋无觅处，得来全不费功夫 (‘you wear out iron shoes tramping in search of it, and then find it without the least effort’) is a well-known proverb—current from the Southern Song writer Xia Yuanding (夏元鼎) and made familiar by its use in 《水浒传》 (Water Margin)—for a thing long sought in vain that turns up by chance. It is corroborated as an attested saying. Here it marks A-Chu’s stumbling, at the Police Bureau, upon the very voice he has hunted.

ch27.anchor: the roaming fish went to meet death without flinching
ch27.note: The chapter title, 踏破冰火九重天 (‘treading through ice and fire, the ninefold heaven’), is the author’s own line in the classical manner rather than a traceable quotation (uncorroborated); 九重天, the ‘ninefold heaven,’ is the highest of the nine tiers of heaven in old Chinese cosmology. The image of passing through ice and fire answers the chapter’s converging perils—a killing at the Police Bureau, Cong Feng walking knowingly into the trap—gathered here in the figure of the roaming fish that goes to meet death without flinching.

ch27.anchor: the peony of Luoyang is first under heaven
ch27.note: Yang Sitong retells a beloved legend: Empress Wu Zetian (武则天, r. 690–705), drunk on a winter night, decreed that every flower bloom by morning; all obeyed but the peony, which would not, and was banished to Luoyang, where it bloomed the more gloriously—whence the saying 洛阳牡丹甲天下 (‘the peony of Luoyang is first under heaven’). The tale is corroborated as a widely told legend (the ‘scorched-boned peony,’ 焦骨牡丹), though it is folklore rather than official history; Wu Zetian’s own fondness for the Luoyang peony is, however, historically attested. Sitong presses it into service to prove that the peony, for all its opulence, has a ‘proud spine’ (傲骨).

ch27.anchor: turn back, and the shore is there
ch27.note: The two men fence in proverbs. Muci’s 回头是岸 (‘turn back, and the shore is there’) is the latter half of the Buddhist admonition 苦海无边，回头是岸 (‘the sea of suffering has no bound; turn back and there is the shore’), a call to repent while there is yet time. Rong Chu returns 水到渠成 (‘when the water comes, the channel forms of itself’), the saying that conditions ripen of their own accord—a serene refusal to turn back.

ch28.note: The chapter title, 间不容发生死际 (‘not a hair’s breadth between, at the very verge of life and death’), turns on the idiom 间不容发, literally ‘the gap will not admit a single hair.’ It is documented in Mei Cheng’s (枚乘) 上书谏吴王 of the Western Han, where a thread bearing a vast weight over an abyss is described — 系绝于天不可复结，坠入深渊难以复出，其出不出，间不容发 — the margin between rescue and ruin narrower than a hair (corroborated). It is the sister image to the 千钧一发 of Han Yu noted at Chapter 21; here the knife-edge is the instant Yu Xiaojiang’s silenced shot decides who lives.

On 18 September 1931 the Japanese Kwantung Army detonated a charge on the South Manchuria Railway near Liutiaohu, outside Shenyang (Mukden), blamed Chinese troops, and used the pretext to overrun the city and, within months, the whole Northeast — the 九一八 or Mukden Incident (corroborated). The puppet state of Manchukuo (伪满) was proclaimed in March 1932. Yu Xiaojiang’s survey of the war dates the scene to the aftermath of these events.

ch28.anchor: A Short History of Chinese Philosophy
ch28.note: The recognition password names Feng Youlan’s (冯友兰) A Short History of Chinese Philosophy, which the Macmillan Company did publish — but in 1948, more than fifteen years after this scene. The book and publisher are real (corroborated); the date makes the reference an anachronism, the author’s rather than the characters’. Here it serves only as the Party’s fallback contact phrase, to be used if anything befell Ronghua.

ch28.anchor: The kite whose string had snapped was joined to its line again
ch28.note: In the source this sentence is followed by a pirate-site watermark line (阳光中文网 www.sunshe.com…), an advertising string injected by the site that scraped the text and no part of the novel. It is kept verbatim in the bilingual QC file but omitted from the reading text, as with the watermark at Chapter 6.

ch29.note: The chapter title, 欲披荒草访疑尘 (‘wishing to part the wild grass to seek out the doubtful dust’), is a seven-character line in the classical manner that traces to no single documented source; like several titles in this book (Chapters 17, 19, 20, 22, 23, 24, 26, 27) it appears to be the author’s own pastiche (uncorroborated). Its wild grass and doubtful dust answer the brothers’ nocturnal survey of the overgrown, long-shunned Ciyun Temple.

ch29.anchor: The China League for Civil Rights
ch29.note: The 中国民权保障同盟 (China League for Civil Rights) was founded in Shanghai in December 1932, led by Song Qingling, Cai Yuanpei and Yang Quan, and campaigned for the release of political prisoners and the safeguarding of civil liberties (corroborated) — which fixes the chapter to its stated ‘winter of 1932.’ Yang Quan was assassinated by Nationalist agents in June 1933, after which the League effectively dissolved.

Wang Jingwei (汪精卫), a senior Nationalist leader, is associated with the slogan of 曲线救国 / 救亡, ‘national salvation by a roundabout path’ — the argument that accommodation with Japan might buy time and preserve the state. It became the byword for his later collaboration: in 1940 he headed a Japanese-sponsored government at Nanjing (corroborated). Du Luning’s sympathy for it marks him, in the novel, as a man already drifting toward the enemy.

ch30.anchor: To die together is a bond well met
ch30.note: The chapter title, 同生共死亲兄弟 (‘brothers, kin in life and death alike’), is a plain seven-character line in the old manner rather than a traceable single quotation (uncorroborated). It is answered by the twins’ exchange in the flooded crypt, 有缘共死，不枉同生 — a bond that turns their forced descent into the trap into the moment they become, in fact as in blood, brothers.

ch30.anchor: when the false is taken for the true, the true becomes false as well
ch30.note: A-Chu quotes 假作真时真亦假, the first line of the couplet inscribed over the Land of Illusion (太虚幻境) in the Dream of the Red Chamber (红楼梦, first noted at Chapter 24); its companion line runs 无为有处有还无, ‘where nothing is made something, the something turns to nothing.’ The couplet’s theme of the true and the false changing places is the engine of this chapter’s buried-identity plot (corroborated).

A 名古屋带 (Nagoya obi) is a lighter, partly pre-folded kimono sash. It is in fact a modern invention, devised in Nagoya around 1920 (which contradicts the source’s tying of it to the 桃山 / Momoyama age of the late sixteenth century; the author uses ‘Momoyama’ loosely for ‘old Japanese’). The bright tubular sash is the detail from A-Chu’s recovered childhood memory that fixes the murderer as a Japanese woman.

ch31.anchor: the hook that will never let go
ch31.note: The chapter title, 游鱼见食不见钩 (‘the roaming fish sees the bait, not the hook’), shapes into a seven-character line the old proverb 人见利而不见害，鱼见食而不见钩 (‘man sees the gain and not the harm; the fish sees the bait and not the hook’), a saying against the greed that blinds one to the trap, current in Qing fiction (it appears in the Jing hua yuan, 镜花缘) and traced back to the Guiguzi (鬼谷子). Corroborated as a proverb, though the exact seven-character form is the author’s own. The whole chapter turns on the figure: A-Chu’s ‘fragrant bait,’ the hook he means to sharpen, and He Yashu’s closing reversal — that she is the hook, and it is he who has bitten.

ch32.anchor: rich wine, a fair woman, the mandarin-duck swords
ch32.note: The chapter title, 醇酒美人鸳鸯剑, fuses two allusions. 醇酒美人 (‘rich wine and a fair woman’) derives from the Records of the Grand Historian (史记, Biography of the Lord of Xinling): dismissed from command, the Lord of Xinling (信陵君) drowned his ruin in strong drink and women (饮醇酒，多近妇女) until it killed him — hence ‘wine and women’ as the road of self-destruction. 鸳鸯剑 (‘the mandarin-duck swords’) are the twin-bladed betrothal sword of the Dream of the Red Chamber (红楼梦), one blade graven 鸳 and its mate 鸯: given by Liu Xianglian to You Sanjie (尤三姐), who cut her own throat with it to prove her honor — the mandarin duck being the emblem of faithful lovers, so the blade stands for love pledged and love turned to death. Both corroborated; the title welds the wine-and-women of a man’s undoing to the lovers’ blade, apt for Koyama Eiko’s seduction of Yang Yuhua and its long, murderous issue.

The anecdote is Plato’s, from the Theaetetus (174a): Thales (泰利士), gazing up at the stars, fell into a well, and a witty Thracian serving-girl laughed that he was so eager to know the heavens he could not see what lay at his feet. Xia Yuechun invokes it by way of coded warning — that A-Chu, intent on the enemy far off, has overlooked the danger at his own side. Corroborated.

ch32.anchor: the deeper its roots reach down into the darkness
ch32.note: A paraphrase of Nietzsche, Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Part I, ‘The Tree on the Mountainside’: ‘it is the same with man as with the tree. The more he seeks to rise into the height and light, the more vigorously do his roots struggle earthward, downward, into the dark and deep — into evil.’ Corroborated. Yang Yuhua takes it as licence for his own descent.

ch32.anchor: It is just because life is short that it seems beautiful
ch32.note: In the source this line of dialogue is followed on the same paragraph by a pirate-site watermark (‘阳光中文网 www.sunshe.com…’), an artefact of the digital text and no part of the novel; it is preserved verbatim in the bilingual QC file but dropped from the reading text. The like was noted at Chapters 6 and 28.

ch32.anchor: On the Distinction of the Three Realms of Civilized and Barbarous
ch32.note: 《文野三界之别》, attributed in the text (at Chapter 33) to Liang Qichao (梁启超, 1873–1929), the reformist thinker. The schema of ‘three realms’ of civilization — the savage (野蛮), the half-opened (半开化), and the civilized (文明) — is indeed Liang’s, set out in his Book of Freedom (自由书) and adapted from Fukuzawa Yukichi’s Outline of a Theory of Civilization. Corroborated as Liang’s idea; that A-Chu should keep such a title on his shelves marks him, to Rong Sheng’s eye later, as no ordinary man.

ch33.anchor: the false holding truth, the true holding falsehood
ch33.note: The chapter title, 假做真时真亦假 (‘when the false is made true, the true too turns false’), is the first line of the couplet over the Land of Illusion (太虚幻境) in the Dream of the Red Chamber, already annotated at Chapter 30 (the standard text reads 假作真时真亦假; this chapter uses the variant 做 for 作). Here the theme is literal: the hypnotist’s craft of mingling true memory with false, and the whole chain of stolen identities the chapter unknots.

ch33.anchor: The Eighteen Nao Songs: Shang Ye
ch33.note: 铙歌十八曲·上邪. ‘Shang Ye’ (上邪, ‘O Heaven!’) is a Han yuefu from the eighteen ‘Nao songs’ (铙歌, drum-and-fife pieces of the 鼓吹曲辞): a woman’s oath of undying love, swearing that only when the hills flatten, the rivers run dry, and thunder sounds in winter snow will she part from her lover. Corroborated. He Yashu’s marking of the passage, and her sending the book to A-Chu, is her own such oath.

ch33.anchor: Snow drifts and drifts on Fuji’s peak; half of this scene belongs to Edo
ch33.note: A-Chu recites the couplet in Japanese to unmask the false Amah A-Yue: the river-plum snow scene embroidered on his shoes resembles the view from the summit of Mount Fuji, and Edo (江户) is the old name of Tokyo, where he has guessed she was raised. 五分 renders idiomatically as ‘half’ (five parts in ten). The lines are the author’s pastiche in the classical Japanese manner rather than a traceable poem (uncorroborated).

ch34.anchor: turned the guest into the host
ch34.note: The chapter title, 反客为主 (‘turn the guest into the host’), is No. 30 of the classical Thirty-Six Stratagems (三十六计): to arrive as a guest and by degrees seize the position of host and master. Here Muci, coming to his brother’s table and his brother’s operation, drugs A-Chu and takes over the endgame against Yang Yuhua, making the stratagem literal; 深造次, ‘a deep rashness,’ names the presumption of it, and 造次 (‘rash, hasty’) sounds again when Xia Yuechun warns Muci not to act rashly.

百川丛惠子, the captured impostor’s true name. As with her fellow agents Koyama Eiko (小山缨子) and Koyama Chino (小山千野), the surname is read in the Japanese manner: 百川 = Momokawa, an attested Japanese surname, and 惠子 is the common given name Keiko. The middle graph 丛 has no settled kana reading, so the whole romanization is provisional. She is a Japanese agent, and not the real Amah A-Yue (岳嬷嬷), whom she murdered twenty years before in order to take her place.

ch34.anchor: the Land Survey Department of the Army General Staff
ch34.note: 陆军测量部参谋本部. The Land Survey Department (陸地測量部) of the Imperial Japanese Army General Staff was the real body charged with military mapping and survey from 1888 to 1945; the covert surveying of Chinese terrain that runs through Keiko’s confession, and the ‘street maps of Shanghai’ found beneath the shrine hall, answer to its actual work. The novel folds its seduction-and-espionage program into this genuine institution (corroborated).

ch35.anchor: Brothers are like geese in flight
ch35.note: The chapter title, 一举锄奸雁归行 (‘at a single stroke the traitor is rooted out, the wild geese return to their rank’), is the author’s own seven-character line in the classical manner rather than a traceable quotation. 雁行, the ordered flight-line of migrating geese, is an old figure for brothers; the closing chapter turns on the two brothers, long divided, at last taking their places side by side, and Young Tang and Yuechun press the same image (兄弟如雁行) to reconcile them.

ch35.anchor: an order given at dawn is answered by dusk
ch35.note: The broadcast the brothers hear is a real wartime statement of the Chinese National Government under Chiang Kai-shek, issued around the fall of Shanghai in November 1937 (in part: 各地战士，闻义赴难，朝命夕至，其在前线以血肉之躯，筑成壕堑，有死无退…实足以昭示民族独立之精神，奠定中华复兴之基础). It is quoted, corroborated, though the exact document and date are given variously in the sources. The passage frames the novel’s close on the eve of the eight-year War of Resistance.

爱中 (Aizhong) and 爱华 (Aihua), the twins’ infant sons, born December 1933. Both names mean, in effect, ‘love China’ (中 and 华 are each names for the country); read together they spell 爱中华, ‘love China.’ The naming lands pointedly four years before the 1937 invasion with which the book ends.

ch35.anchor: May you cherish the one before your eyes
ch35.note: In the linked verse the four friends cap in turn, the line 愿君怜取眼前人 (‘may you cherish the one before your eyes’) echoes the close of Yan Shu’s (晏殊, 991–1055) song-lyric to the tune Huanxi sha: 满目山河空念远，落花风雨更伤春，不如怜取眼前人 (‘a whole land in the eye, and longing for the far away is vain… better to cherish the one before your eyes’). The point is A-Chu’s: he burns the letter from his old love abroad and turns to Yashu, present and living.

格格 (gege) is a Manchu form of address for a daughter of an imperial or noble house — roughly ‘princess’ or ‘young lady of rank’ — used here loosely, as a flattering way of speaking of a well-born Manchu woman.
